narrative: Your application was denied because the model predicted you have a 50.8 percent chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. In other words, the risk of failure was slightly greater than the chance of success, so the school’s decision went against you. The most important factors were academic, and the pattern was clear. Your undergraduate GPA had the strongest influence and it helped you: at 3.40, it was above the 3.23 average among accepted students, pushing the prediction toward passing. But the next two strongest factors pushed the other way. Your third-year class standing was 2 out of 10, far below the accepted-student average of 5.79, and this was a strong signal pointing toward bar exam failure. Your first-year class standing was also 2 out of 10, versus an average of 6.00, adding another strong push toward failure. So even though your undergraduate record was solid, your lower class standing in the first and third years of law school outweighed it. Neither your gender nor race was part of the decision; this was based on your academic profile. Other factors such as family income, LSAT score, and full-time status had less influence. To improve your chances if you reapply, focus on raising your academic standing—consider retaking courses, enrolling in post-baccalaureate work, or seeking academic support—so your transcripts show a stronger upward trend. You could also prepare more intensely for the LSAT. A better record can reduce the predicted risk and lead to a different outcome.
